justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a recent price level around 365–366 for the underlying asset (likely a commodity, index, or ETF trading in that range). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics and no major scheduled catalysts would dramatically shift the market overnight. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 368, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with typical risk-asset behavior in the absence of strong directional signals. At the one-month horizon, I extended that drift further to 372, incorporating a slightly longer-run bullish lean while acknowledging that over four weeks, compounding of small daily moves and any fundamental repricing could push the asset modestly higher.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility patterns at each time horizon. For the one-day window, a range of roughly 23 points (355–378) reflects typical daily price fluctuation scaled conservatively. As I moved to one week and then one month, the intervals widened substantially — from about 46 points at one week to 105 points at one month — because uncertainty compounds over time. Volatility scales approximately with the square root of time, so a one-month interval should naturally be much wider than a one-day interval even under stable conditions.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macro shock — such as an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a disappointing economic data release — could drive prices well below 355 even within a single day. A broader risk-off episode or liquidity crunch could accelerate selling pressure over a week or month. On the upside, stronger-than-expected earnings, a surprise dovish pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices well above 378 or even 425.

The tail risks I am most concerned about are asymmetric in nature. Markets tend to fall faster than they rise, meaning the downside tail at the one-month horizon is arguably fatter than the upside tail, even though I presented symmetric-looking intervals. A black swan event — a credit event, geopolitical shock, or sudden liquidity withdrawal — could push prices 15–20% below my lower bound in a compressed timeframe. Conversely, a powerful momentum rally, particularly if driven by algorithmic or options-related flows, could briefly spike prices beyond my upper bound before reverting. These extremes are low-probability but not negligible.
